- When sentiment is positive (≥ 0.2) in recent days, model tends to under-forecast; increase forecast slightly to align with bullish momentum.  
- When sentiment is negative (≤ -0.1) and price is trending upward, model often over-optimistically peaks; cap forecast at 1–2% below recent high or adjust downward 1–3% to avoid overshoot.  
- If model forecast shows sharp upward spike followed by a steep decline in true outcome, reduce forecast lag by 1–2 days and lower peak value by 3–5% to reflect mean reversion.  
- In cases where true outcome exceeds model by 5%+ over 3–5 consecutive days, apply a “mean reversion bias” — reduce forecast by 1–2% per day until convergence with observed trend.  
- If sentiment history shows repeated negative spikes followed by strong recovery, model often fails to capture the rebound; add 1–3% upward bias to forecast 3–5 days ahead to reflect sentiment-driven momentum.  
- For short-term (1–3 day) forecasts, model tends to lag behind true price; add 0.5–1.5% upward bias to compensate for lag.  
- When sentiment is neutral or mixed (±0.1), model often overfits recent noise; apply smoothing filter or reduce forecast volatility by 10–20% to avoid overreaction.
